architecture.title: Dynamo — disaggregated prefill/decode behind one OpenAI frontend
architecture.caption: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, so Dynamo splits them into separate right-sized pools, routes requests to the worker that already caches the prefix, and lets an SLO Planner grow each pool independently — all behind the same /v1 surface as NIM, vLLM, or Ollama.

sequence.title: One request through disaggregated serving
sequence.caption: The runtime flow the labs measure by hand: prefill produces the KV cache and the first token's latency, NIXL moves that cache to a decode worker, and warm prefix repeats skip prefill entirely.

steps.label: hash the prompt prefix, look up cached workers
NIXL transfers the KV cache over the 200GbE fabric
warm repeat: HIT skips prefill — lab02 sample: cold 780 ms → warm 160 ms TTFT
SLO Planner: worst TTFT breaches 2000 ms at concurrency 4 → grow the prefill pool

charts.title: Dynamo's stacked wins (simulation)
charts.caption: Illustrative factors from this app's sim.py (demos step02/step03) — labeled sim-derived in the tutorial; real value depends on your prefix-sharing rate. Low-QPS, no-shared-prefix workloads don't need Dynamo.

charts.title: Prefill scales with input, decode doesn't
charts.caption: lab01_prefill_vs_decode.py sample expected output (illustrative — measure your own endpoint): TTFT grows 6.3× with input length while decode stays 51.8 vs 50.9 tok/s. That asymmetry is the entire case for disaggregation.

charts.title: SLO ramp — worst TTFT vs the declared objective
charts.caption: lab03_slo_economics.py sample expected output (illustrative): aggregate throughput rose 50.4 → 151.9 tok/s even as TTFT broke the 2000 ms SLO — throughput and latency pull in opposite directions, which is why you declare objectives. At 151.9 tok/s the Spark's 240 W costs ≈$0.0658/1M tokens, electricity only.
